The structures in A×ε around small values of κ in (c) reflect large changes in the relative contributions of the three production diagrams shown in Figure 1.

caption: Diagram showing the different layers of the FELIX software architecture, with the central event loop (shown in green) able to interact with low level network software (supporting RDMA) and operating system signals (including interrupts from the FELIX I/O card). The higher-level layer implements application-specific logic and handles subscriptions from external clients via dedicated sockets, available both in peer-to-peer or publisher/subscriber mode. Sockets can also either operate in "buffered" mode, whereby data are packed into an output buffer before transfer across the network (useful to optimise throughput for small packets) or "unbuffered" mode, where data are transferred immediately (useful for larger packets).

caption: Diagram of the track-finding method used in the FTK. Rounded boxes represent the coarse resolution SuperStrips used to bin the hits from the silicon detectors. Once eight layers (Associative Memory (AM) SuperStrips) with hits match a stored pattern they become a road (solid filled boxes), which is then extrapolated into the remaining four layers (dash-dot filled boxes). One layer may be dropped in the first eight layers used for pattern matching and another in the additional four layers. Fake track candidates (e.g. the gradient-filled boxes to the left) can be rejected because they have a large χ2 value or fail extrapolation to the additional four layers.

caption: (a) A schematic diagram of the digitizer physics. As a MIP traverses the sensor, electrons and holes are created and transported to the electrodes under the influence of electric and magnetic fields. Electrons and holes may be trapped before reaching the electrodes, but still induce a charge on the primary and neighbour electrodes. (b) A flowchart illustrating the components of the digitizer model described in this article. The digitizer takes advantage of pre-computation to re-use as many calculations as possible. For example, many inputs are the same for a given condition (temperature, bias voltage, fluence). The Ramo potential [40,41] only depends on the sensor geometry and the quantities in dashed boxes further depend only on the condition information (see also Section 4.6). The output of the algorithm described in this paper is an induced charge on the primary electrode and the neighbours, which is then converted into a ToT by the existing software.
title: Modelling radiation damage to pixel sensors in the ATLAS detector

caption: Diagram illustrating the process of Smirnov transformation. Rφ is chosen as an example discriminating variable whose distribution is particularly different between electrons and (unconverted) photons. The Rφ probability density function (pdf) in each sample (a) is used to calculate the respective CDF (b). From the two CDFs, a Smirnov transformation can be derived (c). Applying the transformation leads to an Rφ distribution of the transformed electrons which closely resembles the photon distribution (d).

caption: Example dependences of acceptance times efficiency (A×ε) on signal model parameters: (a) mH for the ZH search in the 0L channel, (b) mH for the ZH search in the 2L channel, (c) κ2V and κλ for the non-resonant Vhh search in the 0L channel, and (d) κ2V and κλ for the non-resonant Vhh search in the 1L channel. Each A×ε is calculated relative to, respectively, the νν bbbb, ℓℓ bbbb, νν bbbb, and ℓν final states with ℓ including the e,μ, and τ leptons here. For the resonant VH search, the A×ε is shown without and with the mass requirements on the reconstructed resonances. caption: A schematic diagram illustrating the definition of the EM calorimeter shower shape variable Δ E . The energy deposit of the EM shower in the first layer of the EM calorimeter is displayed, with the horizontal axis showing the position of the strip cell in the η direction, and the vertical axis showing the reconstructed energy deposits in each strip cell. Emax,1S1 is the energy of the strip cell with the largest energy. Emax,2S1 is the energy of the strip cell with the second largest energy. EminS1 is the energy in the strip cell with the lowest energy found between the largest and the second largest energy. Δ E is the difference of the two. The shower shape variable Eratio is a variable closely related to Δ E , and it is defined as the relative difference between Emax,1S1 and Emax,2S1 .

One layer may be dropped in the first eight layers used for pattern matching and another in the additional four layers. Fake track candidates (e.g. the gradient-filled boxes to the left) can be rejected because they have a large χ2 value or fail extrapolation to the additional four layers.

Feynman diagrams for the processes contributing to t-channel single-top-quark production at LO, in the five-flavour scheme. In the dominant subprocess, an up- or down-type quark from one of the colliding protons interacts with a bottom quark or antiquark from the other proton by exchanging a virtual W boson to produce a (a) top quark or (d) top antiquark. In the subdominant subprocess, a down- or up-type antiquark from one of the colliding protons interacts with a bottom quark or antiquark from another proton by exchanging a virtual W boson to produce a (b) top quark or (c) top antiquark.

Example Feynman diagrams of the scalar leptoquark $S_{1}$ model under study, producing a single-top-quark via (a) a non-resonant leptoquark, (b) a resonant leptoquark and (c) a resonant leptoquark with an off-shell leptoquark exchange. The leptoquark $S_{1}$ carries electric charge $Q = -\frac{1}{3}$, spin $S = 1$, lepton number $L = 1$ and baryon number $B = \frac{1}{3}$. In each case, initial states using up or charm quarks are assumed, and a final state consisting of two same-sign muons and one $\tau$-lepton is produced. The charge conjugate of each process is also considered. The dots represent vertices with a leptoquark-to-fermion coupling strength, $\lambda_{ki}$, for the appropriate quark generation ($k$) and lepton generation ($i$).

A schematic diagram of an interaction producing two light-flavour jets and one b-jet, shown in the transverse plane. The lifetime of b-hadrons corresponds to a transverse decay length, L<sub>xy</sub> (typically a few mm), and produces displaced tracks originating from a secondary vertex.  The distance of closest approach of a displaced track to the primary vertex is defined as the transverse impact parameter, d<sub>0</sub>, and typically is large for tracks originating from the decay of b-hadrons.  Conversely, jets initiated by light-flavour quarks or gluons will not exhibit these features and typically contain mostly prompt tracks originating from the primary vertex.

Diagram of the Trigger DataBase schema for Run 3. Table Primary Keys are used to select information from the relevant tables. A Super Master Key links one L1 Menu and one HLT Menu, which in turn each link to many L1 Prescale Sets and HLT Prescale Sets respectively. Prescale Aliases are also linked to the Prescales sets, but in pairs of L1 and HLT keys. Bunch group information is not linked to other tables, but is used at L1 online. HLT Mon Groups are used in offline processing, identified via the Super Master Key. The Schema table is used to identify the DB contents, to enable query searches based on different versions of the schema layout.
